Soc. 2025, 147, 8652−8662 Read Online ACCESS Metrics & More Article Recommendations * sı Supporting Information ABSTRACT: Unclear regulation mechanisms of solid solubility make it difficult to accurately control its concentration, posing challenges for accelerating chemical reactions.
Herein, we use a model system to determine the effects of solvent type and ratio, concentration, and type of lithium salt on sulfur solubility.
Our findings reveal a nonlinear relationship between sulfur solubility and both lithium salt concentration and the ratio of different solvents in composite solutions.
Importantly, significant differences in sulfur solubility are discovered with changes in the solvation structure regulated by the type of salt anion.
Quantitative evaluation of nonlinear sulfur solubility is illustrated to be breaking the threshold value of the interaction energy between the solute and solvent molecules.
Based on these findings, simultaneous regulation of sulfur and lithium polysulfide concentrations in ether electrolytes can be achieved by controlling the concentration and type of salts.

As a result, a liquid−liquid−solid reaction pathway is supported for lithium−sulfur batteries with a finite amount of electrolyte in the coin cell, and the pouch cell shows an energy density of 554 Wh kg−1, ranking at the top level of the reported system. ■INTRODUCTION Regulating the solubility of solid solutes has important applications in many fields such as substance separation1−3 and reaction process regulation.4−6 It plays a crucial role in improving separation process efficiency and reducing costs,7,8 as well as accurately controlling chemical reaction rates.9,10 In 1878, Van’t Hoff studied the relationship between solid solute solubility and temperature and proposed the Van’t Hoff equation.
These results indicate that temperature can regulate solute solubility by changing the intra- and intermolecular forces between solvents and/or solutes.

Compared to the influence of external factors such as temperature and pressure, controlling the internal chemical composition of the solution can provide a more direct way to achieve significant changes in solute solubility by regulating the strength of the interaction forces between the solute and solution components.

For example, Guarr and Hickey et al. showed that the introduction of C−H···π weak dispersion force interactions in pyridiniumbased compounds can weaken intermolecular electrostatic interactions, thus enhancing their solubility in acetonitrile and maximizing the energy density of redox flow battery.11 Therefore, it is very important to precisely control the solid solute concentration to provide an important value for the accurate control of the reaction rate.
However, the influence of solute, solvent, and ion interaction strengths on solute solubility in solution is still needed for a deep understanding.

According to classical theories, the dissolution of solid substances is a competitive process between entropy and enthalpy changes.12 During the dissolution process, breaking the interaction between solvents or solutes is an endothermic process, while constructing the interaction bonds between solutes and solvents is an exothermic process, where the enthalpy change is less than zero.
Therefore, reducing the strength of intermolecular forces between solutes or enhancing the strength of solvent and solute interactions in a solution is key to increasing solute solubility.
Based on this understanding, strategies, including weakening solute interactions and enhancing solvent and solute interactions, have been proposed to regulate solute solubility in solutions.

For example, Yagai et al. demonstrated that the methylation of barbiturate π- conjugated compounds can reduce the intermolecular hydrogen-bonded type of barbiturate solutes and inhibit the formation of polycrystals, thereby improving their solubility in nonpolar solvents.13 Rimer et al. found that the adsorption of citrate inhibitors on the surface of calcium oxalate monohydrate (COM) crystals weakened the interaction of COM solute due to changes in the local lattice strain, thereby increasing the COM concentration in solutions.14 In order to enhance the interaction between solvents and solutes, Received: December 16, 2024 Revised: February 14, 2025 Accepted: February 18, 2025 Published: March 3, 2025 Article pubs.acs.org/JACS © 2025 American Chemical Society 8652 https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.4c17438 J.

In complex mixed solutions, solute solubility may be affected not only by the solvent itself but also by salt anions and cations.
The mechanism for regulating solubility in composite solutions is still unclear, making it difficult to accurately control the solute concentration.

The qualitative and quantitative evaluation of chemical compositions on solute solubility in complex solutions will provide a theoretical basis and technical means for the precise control of the chemical reaction rate and efficiency of substance separation.

Importantly, by comparing the two salts, LiTFSI and LiBr, it is discovered that the solvation structure regulated by the two types of anions has a totally different effect on S8 solubility.

Between them, the solvation structure of LiTFSI with dissociated ion pairs in ether solvents significantly reduces the interaction strength between ether and S8 molecules, while the solvation structure of LiBr with bound ion pairs does not significantly affect the interaction strength between ether and S8 molecules (Figure 1b).

The theoretical results indicate that the obvious change in S8 solubility is directly related to the threshold value of the interaction energy between S8 and the solvent molecules in complex solutions, while the enthalpy change is the core factor affecting S8 solubility.

Based on the above discovery, the precise control of S8 and lithium polysulfide solubility in etherbased electrolytes is achieved by adjusting the concentrations and types (LiTFSI, LiBr, and LiNO3) of lithium salt.

On this basis, a liquid−liquid−solid reaction pathway at the positive electrode of lithium−sulfur (Li−S) batteries is supported (Figure 1c), significantly improving the reaction rate and cell performance.
Coin-type Li−S batteries with a finite amount of electrolyte (electrolyte/sulfur (E/S) ratio of 3 μL mgs −1) show a discharge capacity of 1455 mAh g−1, which is the best value to date.
Moreover, the Li−S pouch cell shows an energy density of 554 Wh kg−1 with 10.77 Ah. ■RESULTS AND DISCUSSION S8 Solubility in a Composite Solution.

The solubility of solid S8 in ether solvents, 1,2-dimethoxyethane (DME), and 1,3-dioxolane (DOL), was primarily studied at room temperature because ethers are commonly used as electrolyte solvents in Li−S batteries.
Raman spectra analysis shows that the solubility of S8 (characteristic peaks: 150, 220, and 456 cm−1)16 is 5.1 mg mL−1 in DOL and 3.65 mg mL−1 in DME (Figure S1).
With the addition of LiTFSI, the solubilities of S8 in DOL solutions containing 0.2, 0.5, 0.8, and 1.0 M LiTFSI are 4.3, 4.0, 3.7, and 1.0 mg mL−1, respectively (Figures 1d and S2).
It was found that S8 solubility decreased slightly with increasing LiTFSI concentration in the range of 0.2−0.8 M.
However, the solubility of S8 decreases sharply when the LiTFSI concentration changes from 0.8 to 1.0 M.
These results indicate that there is a nonlinear solubility phenomenon (Figure 1e).
We also analyzed S8 solubility in DME solvent with 1.0, 0.8, 0.5, and 0.2 M lithium bis(fluorosulfonyl)imide (LiFSI), and a nonlinear solubility phenomenon was also found (Figure S3).

Moreover, in order to further verify the solubility effect of temperature dependence, we tested S8 solubility at 50 °C, which still shows a nonlinear solubility phenomenon, proving its universality (Figure S4).

To illustrate the mechanism of the nonlinear S8 solubility phenomenon in complex solutions with solvents and salts, we used DOL and CS2 as strongly and weakly polarized solvents, respectively, to explore the effect of the mixed solvent ratio on S8 solubility, in which CS2 and DOL serve as good and poor solvents for S8 dissolution, respectively.
This shows that S8 solubilities in DOL and CS2 solvents are about ∼5.1 and ∼60.0 mg mL−1 at room temperature, respectively.
When the molar ratios of CS2 and DOL change to 8:2, 7:3, 6:4, 5:5, 4:6, 3:7, and 2:8, S8 solubilities are 59, 57, 55, 51, 20, 14, and 12 mg mL−1, respectively.
This demonstrates that S8 solubility slightly changes with a change in the ratio of CS2:DOL from 1:0 to 5:5.
However, when the ratio of CS2:DOL changes to 4:6, S8 solubility decreases sharply (20 mg mL−1).
When the ratio further decreases, the solubility changes slightly (Figure 1f).
Furthermore, the measured dielectric constant of the DOL/ CS2 solution shows a nearly linear trend with regard to their ratio, again verifying no relationship between them (Figure 1f).
To check the nonlinear S8 solubility in composite solvents, we used classical molecular dynamics LAMMPS to simulate S8 solubility in DOL/CS2 solvents with different molar ratios.
This shows that S8 solubility in a pure CS2 solvent and mixed CS2/DOL solvent (8:2) is close to 50 mg mL−1.
When the ratio is 5:5, S8 is still in the soluble state (50 mg mL−1).
In contrast, when mixed solvents with a ratio of 2:8 or pure DOL are selected, a large number of S8 molecules precipitate, which is consistent with the experimental results (Figures 1g and S5).

It is worth emphasizing that this nonlinear solubility phenomenon is also found in other systems, for example, the nonlinear solubility of rosin in mixed solvents of water and ethanol (Figures 1h, S6 and S7).
This confirms the broad existence of such phenomena.
To reveal the essence of nonlinear solubility, we analyzed the interaction energy and interaction force between the solvent and solute molecules.
As known, when a solid transforms into a molten liquid, external input interaction energy is needed to reduce the intermolecular forces of the solid.
For example, the interaction energy for the melting heat of S8 from solid to liquid is 1.7175 kJ mol−1.
Similarly, the dissolution of the S8 solute in the solvent also requires the input of interaction energy to reduce the interaction forces of S8 molecules in the solid.
When S8 solute dissolves in solvents, the required interaction energy comes from the van der Waals forces formed between the solvent and S8 molecules.
For S8 dissolution in CS2-DOL solvents, CS2 and DOL act as good and poor solvents for S8 dissolution, respectively.
S8 solubility will quickly decrease when the interaction force of the mixed solvents and S8 is weaker than the interaction force of the two S8 molecules.
We use the classical molecular dynamics simulation method (LAMMPS) to calculate the interaction energy.

According to the constructed model, we obtain the average interaction energy of the extra input to dissolve one S8 molecule (Edis or Edis′, and the calculation details of Edis and Edis′ are shown in Supporting Note 2).
The average energy released from the interaction of one CS2 molecule and one S8 molecule is Ea, and the energy released from one DOL molecule and one S8 molecule is Eb (Eb < Ea).
When the average action energy of the solvent on the solute is greater than the average energy required for the solute to dissociate a molecule, the solubility of the solute will be high.
Therefore, if xEa + yEb < Edis (Edis′) is satisfied, S8 will precipitate.
Herein, x and y are the coordinated numbers of the CS2 and DOL molecules on the S8 molecule.
According to the calculation results (details in Supporting Note 2), Ea is 3.28 × 10−2 kcal mol−1, Eb is 1.1 × 10−2 kcal mol−1, and Edis is 1.2198 kcal mol−1 (Edis′ = 1.48 kcal mol−1).

Moreover, the relationship between the average energy of one solute molecule and the molar ratio of the two solvents can be obtained by the equation = + y 2.329 x 1.548 1, and the solubility mutation of S8 in the mixed system of CS2 and DOL will be between the ratio of CS2 to DOL of 3:7 and 4.54:5.45.
In the experiment, the proportion of solubility mutation measured in the CS2 and DOL mixed system is 4:6, which is just within the proportion range of our theoretical deduction.
This proves the reliability of the calculation theory for this system.

S8 solubility in CS2 is evaluated to be ∼60 mg mL−1 at room temperature.
This means that one S8 molecule dissolves into 71 CS2 molecules.
That is, the average solvation structure of CS2 and S8 can be hypothesized to be a 71-bound structure (71 CS2−S8).
With CS2 as the pure solvent, the interaction energy released from 71 CS2 molecules and one S8 molecule is 71*Ea (2.329 kcal mol−1).
Because 71*Ea > Edis (2.329 > 1.2198) and 71*Ea > Edis′ (2.329 > 1.48) are present, the solubility of S8 in the CS2 solvent is high.
When the ratio of CS2 to DOL is 5:5, the interaction energy released from 35.5 CS2 and 35.5 DOL molecules to one S8 molecule is 35.5*Ea + 35.5*Eb (1.555 kcal mol−1).

Because 35.5*Ea + 35.5*Eb > Edis (1.555 > 1.2198) and 35.5*Ea + 35.5*Eb > Edis′ (1.555 > 1.48) are still present, S8 solubility in the CS2/DOL (5:5) solvents is also high (about 51 mgS mL−1), which is a little lower than that in pure CS2.
In stark contrast, when the ratio of CS2 to DOL is 4:6, the interaction energy released from 28.4 CS2 and 42.6 DOL molecules to one S8 molecule is 1.40 kcal mol−1.
Because this value is lower than Edis′ (1.40 < 1.48), there is a significant difference in S8 solubility (about 20 mg mL−1), which is much lower than that in CS2 (Figure 1f,g).

The above estimation of input interaction energy for solute dissolution in a solvent can explain the nonlinear solubility phenomenon well, confirming that the enthalpy change is the core factor affecting S8 solubility in this system (Figures 1i and S8).

The interaction energy for the fast change in solute solubility, which is due to breaking intramolecular forces of the solute through the intermolecular action between solvent and solute, relates to the threshold value of the interaction energy.
Effect of LiTFSI Concentration on S8 Solubility and Cathode S Reactions.

It is worth noting that in a mixed solvent of DME/DOL (1:1), there is also a nonlinear solubility result when the LiTFSI concentration changes from 0.8 to 1.0 M (Figure S9).
At a scan rate of 0.05 mV s−1, the CV curves show two reduction peaks (EPc1, S8 →Li2S4 and EPc2, Li2S4 →Li2S) and two oxidation peaks (EPa2, Li2S →Li2Sx and EPa1, Li2Sx → S8).

Compared to that with 1.0 M LiTFSI, the calculated activation energy of S8 →Li2S8 in the presence of 0.8 M LiTFSI reduces by 37.24 kJ mol−1 (Figure S13b), confirming the accelerated reaction due to S8 dissolution with a decreased amount of unpolarized ether molecules.

When the CV scan rate further increases to 0.15 mV s−1, the first Pc1 reduction peak potential with 0.8 M LiTFSI shows a positive shift, and the current response with 0.8 M LiTFSI (1.91 mA) is larger than that with 1.0 M LiTFSI (1.21 mA) (Figure 2c).

In one previous study of Li−S batteries at the condition of high S loading and low E/S ratio performed by our group,17 we found that the rate of the S ↔Li2S interconversion reaction was controlled by the activation of S8 in the first S8 →Li2S8 step.

The S8 activation ratio (Sact) can be determined by evaluating the actual and theoretical quantity ratios of the transferred electrons of the S8 →Li2S4 reaction (Sact = Eactual(S8 →Li2S4)/Etheorectical (S8→Li2S4)).

Moreover, the S8 utilization ratio (Suti) can be determined by evaluating the actual and theoretical quantity ratios of the transferred electrons of the total S8 →Li2S reaction, Suti = Eactual(S8 →Li2S)/Etheorectical(S8 →Li2S).
The detailed calculation can be found in ref 17.
The changes in Sact and Suti can be used as descriptors to evaluate the increased factor of the reaction rate for the total S reduction reaction.
Then, we calculated Sact and Suti at different scan rates to quantitatively evaluate the increase of the reaction rate (Figure 2d,e).
At a low scan rate of 0.05 mV s−1, Sact and Suti values were calculated to be 50 and 50% at 0.8 M LiTFSI, respectively, which are higher than those with 1 M LiTFSI (41.7 and 40%).
At a scan rate of 0.1 mV s−1, Sact and Suti values (45 and 23%) with 0.8 M LiTFSI are much higher than those with 1 M LiTFSI (32 and 13%).
These results demonstrate that the electrolyte with 0.8 M LiTFSI can achieve effective S dissolution and thus increase the reaction rate (Figure 2g,h).
This reaction pathway was further proven by the S8 solubility test on a solid substrate (Figures S14 and S15).
However, note that the second Pc2 reduction peak with 0.8 M LiTFSI cannot appear well at a scan rate of 0.15 mV s−1, and the Sact and Suti values are also very low.
This indicates a low reaction rate, which may be related to the limited Li2Sx amount in 0.8 M LiTFSI-based electrolyte during the redox reactions.
In order to confirm the above processes, we investigated the disproportionation reaction rates of S and Li2S in ether electrolytes with 1.0 and 0.8 M LiTFSI (DOL/DME = 2:1, v/ v).

Due to the long reaction time and volatilization of the ether solvent, the Li2Sx solution in DOL/DME (1:1) is highly viscous, and it cannot accurately evaluate the disproportionation reaction and Li2Sx solubility at different time scales.
Therefore, we used DOL/DME solvent at a ratio of 2:1 (v/v) to determine the formation rate of Li2Sx (Figure S16).
The optical photographs show that the color of the Li2Sx solution with 0.8 M LiTFSI diluted 200 times is darker than that with 1.0 M LiTFSI in the primary state.
In the ultraviolet−visible (UV−vis) spectra, the intensity of the absorption peak of S4 2− (420 nm) is also higher than that with 1.0 M LiTFSI.
These results demonstrate that the increase of S8 solubility accelerates the disproportionation reaction and the generation of Li2Sx (Figure S17).
We further determined Li2Sx concentrations at different time scales, and the higher concentration of Li2Sx solution with 0.8 M LiTFSI was found in the primary 0−16 h.
However, after 16 h, the concentration of the Li2Sx solution with 1.0 M LiTFSI is higher than that with 0.8 M LiTFSI (Figures 2f and S18).
It may be due to the fact that more Li+ formed Li3S6 + with Li2S6 when the LiTFSI concentration is 1.0 M.

In short, due to the insulation property of S/Li2S, the conventional solid−liquid−solid reaction path with limited long-range electron transfer occurs in the electrolyte with a limited amount of unpolarized ether (1 M LiTFSI, Figure 2j).

In stark contrast, due to the improved S8 solubility in the electrolyte with an increased amount of unpolarized ether (0.8 M LiTFSI), the liquid−liquid−solid reaction pathway with an enhanced long-range electron transfer route is constructed.
Accelerated Reaction Probed by In Situ Raman Spectra.
To confirm the liquid−liquid−solid reaction pathway initiated by the increased S8 solubility, we used in situ Raman spectroscopy to probe the cathode reaction process of Li−S batteries.
At a discharge current density of 1C, the S8 peaks located at 220 and 476 cm−1 appear at the open-circuit voltage (OCV).
With 1 M LiTFSI in the electrolyte, S8 peaks can still be detected at a discharge voltage of 2.40 V.
In addition, the weak Li2Sx peaks (398 and 450 cm−1)18 can be detected at 2.35 V, and Li2Sx can still be detected at a discharge voltage of 1.86 V (Figure 3a).
This suggests that the reduction reaction rate is low and S is not completely reduced.
In contrast, the S8 peak cannot be detected at 2.40 V with 0.8 M LiTFSI in the electrolyte, and Li2Sx peaks can be detected at 2.40 V, much earlier and stronger than those with 1.0 M LiTFSI.
Moreover, Li2Sx peaks completely disappear at 1.91 V, indicating complete S reduction due to a greatly increased reaction rate (Figure 3c).
Compared to the discharge capacity of the battery with 1.0 M LiTFSI (746 mAh g−1), the higher value with 0.8 M LiTFSI (928 mAh g−1) also indicates a faster reaction rate (Figure 3b,d).
Similar to the discharge process, with 1 M LiTFSI, the Li2Sx peaks can be detected at a potential of 2.38 V during the charging process, relating to the high charging potential (Figure 3e).
No S8 substance was observed at the end of charging, indicating a low reaction rate.
However, with 0.8 M LiTFSI, a strong Li2Sx peak can be detected at a charging potential of 2.35 V, 30 mV earlier than that with 1 M LiTFSI (Figure 3g).
Moreover, the S8 peaks appear at 2.80 V.
This indicates a higher reaction rate of 0.8 M LiTFSI than that of 1 M LiTFSI, consistent with their different charging voltages (Figure 3f,h).

To further clarify the effect of increased S8 solubility on the reaction pathway, we performed morphological analysis to illustrate the nucleation and growth of Li2S by using scanning electron microscopy (SEM).
With 1.0 M LiTFSI, a thin layer of Li2S film deposits appears on the electrode surface at the initial growth stage (Figure S19a).
With the increase of discharge depth, the film-like Li2S gradually covers the electrode surface (Figure S19b).
This indicates that Li2S tends to grow in a two-dimensional mode in the presence of 1 M LiTFSI.
In contrast, with 0.8 M LiTFSI, at the initial Li2S deposition stage, it shows a three-dimensional growth of island-shaped Li2S (Figure S19c).
With the increase of discharge depth, these deposits turn into spherical structures, and most of the electrode surface remains clean (Figure S19d).

Studies have shown that lowering the lithium salt concentration can induce the Li2S deposition mode from transient nucleation to continuous nucleation.19 These results demonstrate that an increase of S8 solubility in the electrolyte by increasing the amount of unpolarized ether molecules converts the original solid−liquid−solid into the liquid−liquid−solid reaction pathway for better S8 utilization.
Effect of Lithium Salt Types on S8 Solubility and Cathode Reactions.

It should be noted that the solubility of Li2Sx in the electrolyte with 1.0 M LiTFSI is higher than that with 0.8 M LiTFSI, possibly because more Li+ in 1.0 M LiTFSI increases the formation of Li3S6 + positive ions or polarized ether molecules, promoting the amount of dissolved Li2Sx species.
However, when 1 M LiTFSI is used, S8 solubility sharply decreases to about 1.0 mg mL−1.
Therefore, it seems contradictory to have an ether electrolyte with both good S8 and Li2Sx solubility in the presence of LiTFSI.
However, such an electrolyte is definitely important to achieve high reaction kinetics for Li−S batteries with high-energy densities.

Raman spectra analysis shows that there is no obvious effect of LiNO3 on S8 solubility in DOL solutions, and there is also a nonlinear relation between S8 solubility with 0.8 to 1.0 M LiTFSI (Figures 4c and S20), similar to that of LiBr.
We further analyzed the dielectric constant of the electrolyte, demonstrating that S8 nonlinear solubility is also independent of the dielectric constant (Figure 4c).

We further investigated the soluble state of S8 in DOL in the presence of 1 M LiTFSI or 1 M LiBr by using classical molecular dynamics LAMMPS simulations.
As shown in Figure 4d−f, ten S8 molecules dissolve in DOL but precipitate in DOL with 1 M LiTFSI.
However, ten S8 molecules are dissolved in DOL in the presence of 1 M LiBr, proving that LiBr had no negative effect on S8 solubility.
Moreover, ten S8 molecules are dissolved in DOL with 0.8 M LiTFSI in the presence of LiBr, consistent with the experimental results (Figure S21).

In order to further explore the mechanism by which LiBr, LiNO3, and LiTFSI have different influences on S8 solubility in ether solvents, the electrostatic potential distributions and Mulliken layout analysis of the solvated structures formed by LiBr and LiTFSI in DOL were calculated (Figure 4g−i).
The results show that in the solvated structures of LiTFSI and DOL, the DOL molecule is strongly polarized (Figure 4h).
The charge density of the original two oxygen atoms is significantly changed, and the corresponding valence charges change from −0.2359 and −0.2488 to −0.1940 and −0.3092, respectively.

The valence charges of the original two oxygen atoms only change to −0.2983 and −0.3130 (Figure 4i).
This means that DOL molecules are strongly polarized by LiTFSI, but DOL is weakly polarized by LiBr (Figure 4j).

To evaluate the effect of LiBr on the formation rate of Li2Sx, we investigated the disproportionation reaction rate of S and Li2S in the presence of 0.8 M LiTFSI and 0.2 M LiBr in the electrolyte (DOL/DME = 2:1, v/v).
The optical photographs show that the color of the solution with 0.8 M LiTFSI and 0.2 M LiBr after 200 times dilution is darker than that with 0.8 M LiTFSI.
In the UV−vis spectra, the intensity of the S4 2− absorption peak (420 nm) is higher than that with 0.8 M LiTFSI.
The results show that the addition of LiBr can accelerate Li2Sx formation during disproportionation reactions (Figure S22).
We further continued to test soluble Li2Sx concentrations at different time scales.

With an increased reaction time, the Li2Sx amount in the presence of 0.8 M LiTFSI and 0.2 M LiBr is also higher than that with 1.0 M LiTFSI, suggesting the promotion effect of LiBr on Li2Sx formation (Figure 4k).

In addition, DFT calculations show that the solvated structures formed by LiBr and DOL can stabilize Li2S4 through dipole interactions with a binding energy of −123.46 kJ mol−1 (Figure S23), confirming the stabilization effect of LiBr on Li2Sx.
To evaluate the effect of LiBr on the cathode reaction rate, we performed a CV test with 0.8 M LiTFSI electrolyte in the presence and absence of 0.2 M LiBr.
At a scan rate of 0.05 mV s−1 and an E/S of 5 μL mgs −1, the CV curves are similar in the presence and absence of LiBr.
This reveals that the amount of Li2Sx generated in the two electrolytes is high at a low current rate to ensure the high extent of S ↔Li2S interconversion reactions (Figure S24a).
At a scan rate of 0.1 mV s−1, the first Pc1 peak positively shifts, and the peak current density increases in the presence of LiBr compared to that without LiBr.
The difference in the second Pc2 reduction peak is more obvious.
In the presence of LiBr, the peak potential shows a positive shift of about 80 mV and the peak current increases from 3.12 to 4.86 mA (Figure S24b).
Tafel slopes and activation energy calculations further confirm the increase of the reaction rate (Figure S25a,b).
At a CV scan rate of 0.15 mV s−1, the introduction of LiBr accelerates the total reaction pathway.
The battery with 0.8 M LiTFSI shows only one reduction peak, but the battery with 0.8 M LiTFSI and 0.2 M LiBr shows two distinct reduction peaks (Figure 4l).
This proves that LiBr can increase the total reaction rate.

The above results demonstrate that an increase of S8 solubility effectively increases the reaction rate, and LiBr with an associated ion pair can stabilize Li2Sx to further accelerate the reaction without sacrificing S8 dissolution in the ether electrolyte.
Based on this finding, we assembled a Li−S battery.
At an S loading of 5.0 mg cm−2 and an E/S ratio of 10 μL mgs −1, we evaluated the rate performance (Figure 5a).
The battery with 0.8 M LiTFSI and 0.2 M LiBr show discharge capacities of 1328.8, 1030.4, 955.5, and 607.9 mAh g−1 at current rates of 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, and 0.5 C, respectively.
All these values are much higher than those obtained with 1 M LiTFSI.
The polarization voltage at different discharge rates is also much lower than that with 1 M LiTFSI (Figure S26), indicating a greatly improved reaction rate.
The charge− discharge curve (Figure 5b) shows that two typical discharge platforms can be clearly observed for the battery with 0.8 M LiTFSI and 0.2 M LiBr at a current rate of 0.5C.
However, the disappearance of the second platform of the battery with 1 M LiTFSI (Figure S27) further indicates the lower reaction rate of the battery with 1.0 M LiTFSI.
To further evaluate the cell performance, we measured the cycling performance (current density of 0.5C) at an S loading of 2.18 mg cm−2 and an E/S ratio of 10 μL mgs −1.

The capacity of the battery with 0.8 M LiTFSI and 0.2 M LiBr is significantly higher than that of the 1 M LiTFSI battery, and the cycle time is about 2.3 times that of the 1 M LiTFSI battery (Figure S28).
In addition, the polarization voltage at different cycles is lower than that with 1 M LiTFSI (Figure S29).

To evaluate its application under high S loading and low E/S ratio, we further measured the cycling performance (a current density of 0.2C) at an S loading of 4.25 mg cm−2 and an E/S ratio of 5 μL mgs −1 (Figure 5c).
The initial discharge capacity of the battery with 0.8 M LiTFSI and 0.2 M LiBr at 0.05C (first-circle activation) is up to 1456 mAh g−1, which is much higher than that with 1 M LiTFSI (1251 mAh g−1).

At a current density of 0.2C, the discharge capacity of the battery with 0.8 M LiTFSI and 0.2 M LiBr is 1104 mAh g−1, while that with 1.0 M LiTFSI is 219 mAh g−1, and the second platform of the battery with 1 M LiTFSI disappears (Figure S30).
After 100 cycles, the battery with 0.8 M LiTFSI and 0.2 M LiBr still has a discharge capacity of 883 mAh g−1, with an average capacity decay rate of only 0.2% (Figure 5d).
The second platform was still visible after 200 cycles (Figure S31).
To further demonstrate its application under harsh conditions, we assembled Li−S batteries with an S loading of 6.2 mg cm−2 and an E/S ratio of 3 μL mgs −1.
The battery with 0.8 M LiTFSI and 0.2 M LiBr has a high initial discharge capacity of 1129 mAh g−1 at 0.1C and can be operated stably over 70 cycles (Figure 5e).
In contrast, the second platform at 0.05 and 0.1C cannot be observed for the battery with 1 M LiTFSI, and a capacity of 171.6 mAh g−1 is achieved at a low current of 0.05C (Figure S32).

In order to verify the practicality of Li−S batteries with the designed electrolyte, a pouch cell with a level of 10.77 Ah was assembled, in which an S load of 4.6 mg cm−2 (single side) at the positive electrode and an E/S ratio of 3 μL mgs −1 were selected.
The discharge capacity of 1421 mAh g−1 in the first circle at 0.1C is achieved, corresponding to an energy density of 554 Wh kg−1 (Figure 5f,g).
The decreased capacity during cell cycling may be due to Li metal corrosion under harsh conditions with a low electrolyte volume.
We evaluated the long cycle performance of the Li//Li symmetric battery with 0.8 M LiTFSI and 0.2 M LiBr (Figure S33).
The cells can stably cycle, proving that LiBr has no obvious effect on the cycling performance of the Li metal electrode.
However, more focus should be paid to Li metal protection in future research, as we found some damage to the Li metal electrode after battery cycling (Figure S34).

Sublimed sulfur (S), lithium nitrate (LiNO3), rosin(C19H29COOH) and carbon disulfide (CS2) were purchased from Aladdin (Shanghai, China); Lithium bromide (LiBr), Lithium sulfide (Li2S) were purchased from Macklin (Shanghai, China); 1,2-dimethyl ether (DME), 1,3-diamethoxyethane (DOL) and bis(trifluoromethanesulfony)imide lithium salt (LiTFSI) were purchased from Dodochem(Suzhou, China).

Preparation of S loading cathode.
The pyrrole was added to the 0.5 M ferric chloride (FeCl3) solution and stirred for 12 h to obtain polypyrrole.

After drying, a certain mass of potassium hydroxide (KOH) (the mass ratio of polypyrrole to KOH was 1:4) was weighed and dissolved with distilled water, then added to the polypyrrole, and stirred for more than 30 min to make it to the slurry form.
After drying in an oven, the above mixture was heated at 800 °C for 1 hours with a nitrogen atmosphere to obtain porous carbon (PC).
Then, the PC and S8 (S) were mixed and grinded at a mass ratio of 3:7, and then heated at 155 °C for 12 hours under vacuum to obtain the sulfur porous carbon composite (S-PC).

Carbon fiber (10 wt%), S-PC powder (80 wt%) and poly(vinylidene fluoride) (10 wt%) as a binder were dispersed in Nmethyl-2- pyrrolidone (NMP) to form a slurry, and then coated onto an aluminum (Al) foil and dried using a coating machine with different coating thicknesses and dride at 60 °C for 24 h under vacuum.
Finally, the cathodes were formed.

Electrolyte and polysulfide preparation. 1.0 M lithium bis(trifluoromethanesulfony)imide (LiTFSI) and 0.3 M lithium nitrate (LiNO3) dissolved in 1,3-dioxetane (DOL)/ 1,2- diamethoxyethane (DME) (v/v=1:1) mixed solvents was adopted as the blank electrolyte. 0.8, 0.5 and 0.2M LiTFSI or 0.8 M LiTFSI/0.2 M LiBr and 0.3 M lithium nitrate (LiNO3) dissolved in 1,3-dioxetane (DOL)/1,2-diamethoxyethane (DME) (v/v=1:1) mixed solvents were prepared.
The mixtures of lithium sulfides (Li2S) and sulfur (S) with a molar ratio of 1:5 and 1:7 were added into DOL/DME mixed solvents.
Then the powder was heated under an argon (Ar) atmosphere at 60 °C to prepare Li2S6 and Li2S8.
